description_full: Aritzia Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, develops, and sells apparels and accessories for women in the United States and Canada. The company offers activewear, blazers and vests, dresses, intimates and shapewear, jackets and coats, jeans, lounge wears, pants, bodysuits, tanks, shirts and blouses, shorts, skirts, sweaters and cardigans, sweatpants, sweatshirts and hoodies, denim, and sweat suits, as well as t-shirts, and tops. It also provides accessories, such as bags, belts, hats, scarves and ties, and socks; and sweat fleece and shorts; graphics; leggings; and bra tops. The company offers its products under the Aritzia, Fred Segal, Babaton, Wilfred free, Reigning Champ, The Super Puff, Denim Forum, The Group, Golden, Little Moon, Sunday Best, Ten, Tna, Wilfred, Contour, Crepette, Sweatfleece, The Effortless Pant, The Limitless Pant, The Lodge Pant, Everyday Luxury, and HomeStretch brands. It sells its products through digital channels and boutiques. The company was formerly known as Aritzia Capital Corporation and changed its name to Aritzia Inc. in August 2016. Aritzia Inc. was founded in 1984 and is headquartered in Vancouver, Canada.

financial_summary: Aritzia Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $12.4B market cap on $2.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 10% cost of capital, a 5-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 42%.

The business throws off $380M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -14.1% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 9.3×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 14% operating margin runs 7pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 28% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 47% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market.
About $3.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $91.82 (margin of safety -20%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 4%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $47.51 to $172 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 30.7 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 16.0 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 32.7 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 20.7% annual cash-flow growth, 3pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 15% earns above the cost of capital of 10.1%, but the 5pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.41).
It runs a 42% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 2.15x, but high accruals (-14.1% of assets).
ROE of 28% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
SG&A jumped 28% last year, worth watching.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.5x net debt to EBITDA ($419.1M of cash against $704.8M of debt), with interest covered 9.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.9% over 3 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 59% of profits supports about 8.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 16.8% on average.
Analysts expect 21.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 42%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (1.2% in buybacks).
people: With about 8,800 employees, each generates about $298K of revenue, 0.8x the Consumer Cyclical median.
That works out to $43K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $4.3M (14x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
